title: Appeals Court Backs GOP Redistricting Plan in Missouri, Setting Up Supreme Court Showdown
snippet: A federal appeals court has ordered Missouri to use a heavily Republican-favored congressional map for the upcoming elections, though a one-week stay guarantees a final clash at the U.S. Supreme Court.
content:
JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. — A federal appeals court has ordered Missouri to implement a Republican-drawn congressional map for the upcoming general election, handing state conservatives a major legal victory while teeing up yet another high-stakes battle at the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Monday that forcing state election officials to rely on an older redistricting layout violates the U.S. Constitution. However, the appellate panel placed its decision on hold for seven days, granting voting rights groups and opponents a brief window to petition the nation's highest court for emergency intervention.

A Fractured Legal Battleground

The ruling marks the latest escalation in a protracted legal tug-of-war over Missouri's eight congressional seats. The state Supreme Court had previously blocked the legislature's 7-1 Republican-leaning plan following a constitutional referendum challenge, directing state election administrators to fall back on an older 6-2 map arrangement.

That back-and-forth created unprecedented confusion ahead of the general election, particularly because Missouri's primary elections were conducted using the newer 7-1 map before state courts stepped in.

Appellate Judges Cite Voter Confusion and Disenfranchisement

In siding with conservative plaintiffs, the 8th Circuit highlighted the severe logistical and constitutional harms of switching maps mid-election cycle. The judges pointed to conservative estimates showing that forcing the state to use the older map would effectively disenfranchise voters statewide.

According to the ruling, reverting to the former boundaries would leave more than 1.4 million Missourians unable to vote for the district nominees who appeared on their primary ballots, while over a quarter-million voters cast primary votes for candidates who would no longer be eligible to represent them.

A primary target of the GOP-authored redistricting plan is the 5th Congressional District, currently represented by veteran Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver. The contested map carves up Cleaver's traditional Democratic base in Kansas City, stretching the district into rural, heavily Republican territory.

Voting Rights Advocates Push Back as Election Commences

The court's decision drew immediate fire from grassroots coalitions behind the referendum push, who pointed out that election operations are already well under way across the state.

"Ballots have been printed, and Missourians have already voted," said People Not Politicians, the campaign group fighting the GOP-drawn boundaries, in a statement responding to the decision. "Thousands more will vote before this order seeks to take effect. Officials should stop wasting taxpayers’ money on pointless legal action and instead focus on administering our elections."

With the 8th Circuit's one-week stay now ticking down, the dispute heads back to the U.S. Supreme Court, which will have the final say on which map governs Missouri's congressional races this fall.
